title: Project Overview — Secure Multi-Agent AI Framework for RAN Control Loops
content: The project develops a secure multi-agent AI framework for 6G Radio Access Network control loops under the Nokia Bangalore University Collaboration. The current prototype uses seven MAPPO agents associated with a seven-cell hexagonal RAN scenario. The main implemented control problem is RRC handover decision-making. Security components address Byzantine action corruption, anomaly detection, dynamic trust, policy checking, and consensus diagnostics. The project is structured as a lightweight Python RAN simulation plus learned multi-agent controllers and a dashboard.

title: Project Scope — What Is Actually Implemented
content: The strongest implemented end-to-end path is seven-agent MAPPO handover control with a Python RAN environment, MATLAB-generated channel maps, Byzantine fault injection, anomaly detection, trust scoring, and dashboard visualization. Access control, resource allocation, beamforming, QoS, and other RRC/network decisions are part of the broader framework vision and are represented in the supervised baseline, but they should not be described as fully implemented MARL control loops unless the corresponding code is present and evaluated.

title: Why Reinforcement Learning over LLMs for RAN Control
content: The project prioritizes reinforcement learning for the low-level RRC control loop because handover decisions are time-sensitive and need predictable, lightweight inference after training. LLM-based agents were considered more appropriate for higher-level reasoning, threat analysis, orchestration, or operator assistance where latency is less restrictive. This is a system-design choice rather than a claim that LLMs are universally unsuitable for telecom networks.

title: MAPPO — Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization
content: MAPPO stands for Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization. The implementation follows the centralized-training/decentralized-execution idea: training can use global information through a centralized critic while each actor makes a local decision from its own observation during execution. The seven-agent setup is intended to learn coordinated behavior without requiring a single centralized policy to directly control every UE.

title: RRC and Handover Control
content: Radio Resource Control (RRC) is a control layer responsible for connection and mobility-related procedures between the UE and radio network. In this prototype, the learned agents focus on handover triggering. A handover moves a UE's serving connection from one cell to another. Triggering too early can cause unnecessary switching and ping-pong behavior; triggering too late can allow signal quality to deteriorate and contribute to radio link failure.

title: RAN Scenario and Seven-Cell Layout
source: PESU MARL Implementation — MATLAB channel model
content: The simulated RAN uses seven hexagonal cells in a 1 km by 1 km area with an inter-site distance of approximately 500 m. Each agent corresponds to one cell in the seven-agent experiment. User equipment moves through the environment and observes local radio conditions. The channel model is precomputed and queried during simulation rather than calculating full physical-layer propagation from scratch at every RL step.

title: MATLAB Channel Model Dataset
content: Synthetic channel maps were generated using a 3GPP TR 38.901 Urban Macro-style path-loss setup over the seven-cell scenario. The project uses rsrp_map.csv and sinr_map.csv. RSRP values represent received reference-signal power from the cells at positions in the simulation grid. SINR values represent signal quality after accounting for interference and noise. The maps are queried by the Python environment to provide channel conditions for the RL simulation.

title: Nokia 70k Telemetry Dataset
content: The project contains a Nokia-provided telemetry CSV with approximately 70,000 rows. It is used primarily for the supervised-learning baseline, dashboard data exploration, and validation of security-related analytics. The dataset contains radio/network telemetry and labeled target fields used by the baseline agents. The exact meaning and provenance of every column should be taken from dataset_metadata.json or the project README rather than inferred from column names alone.

title: RAN Environment — Python Simulation
content: The project uses a lightweight Python RAN simulator with a multi-agent environment interface. The environment models seven cells and moving UEs. At each timestep, the environment updates UE/channel state, obtains radio features from the channel maps, receives an action from each agent, applies the security/control logic used by the selected training configuration, and calculates rewards. This avoids the setup overhead of a full network simulator while keeping the research focus on multi-agent control and security.

title: Observation Space
content: The current handover environment uses a compact local observation consisting of SINR, delta RSRP, and NACK density. SINR describes radio quality relative to interference and noise; delta RSRP captures relative signal strength information; NACK density provides an indication of recent transmission problems. These features are used by the MAPPO actor as local state information.

title: Action Space
content: The handover controller uses three high-level actions: defer, trigger handover to the best candidate neighbor, or trigger handover to the second-best candidate neighbor. The exact integer/action encoding should be taken from the environment implementation rather than assumed from the semantic names. In secure training, a compromised action can be corrupted before execution, and a sufficiently low-trust agent can be forced to defer.

title: Reward Function Design
content: The handover reward is designed around useful mobility decisions. A successful handover to a materially better cell receives a positive reward, healthy defer in a stable region receives a smaller positive reward, radio link failure receives a strong negative reward, and unnecessary ping-pong switching receives a negative reward. The exact values used in the current experiments are +10 for successful handover, +1 for healthy defer, -10 for radio link failure, and -5 for ping-pong. Secure training can additionally incur security-related costs when compromised actions affect execution.

title: Experiment 1 — Supervised ML Baseline
content: Experiment 1 is our supervised machine-learning baseline. It uses 8 independent classification and regression agents trained on the 70k-row RAN telemetry dataset. The test results are: mobility F1 0.903, security F1 0.994, resource R2 0.406, energy F1 1.000, trust R2 0.558, beamforming R2 -0.001, QoS F1 0.894, and policy F1 0.837. This baseline predicts labels or values from static telemetry snapshots; it does not perform sequential decision-making or adversarial RL training. It is used to provide a conventional ML reference point for evaluating the MARL approach.

title: Experiment 1 — Why It Is Not Directly Comparable to RL
content: The supervised baseline predicts labels or values from static telemetry rows. It does not interact with an environment over sequential timesteps, learn a policy from reward, or experience simulated Byzantine attacks during its prediction loop. Therefore F1/R2 from Experiment 1 should be presented as baseline predictive performance, while RL experiments should be evaluated using reward, handover outcomes, radio link failures, and security metrics.

title: Experiment 2 — MAPPO Without Security
content: Experiment 2 trains seven MAPPO agents for 1000 episodes without the security layer. The reported 50-episode moving-average reward improves from roughly 867 in early training to roughly 1791 late in training. Deterministic evaluation reports reward 962, 386 successful handovers, and zero radio link failures. The run was described as converging cleanly without major instability.

title: Experiment 3 — MAPPO Plus Security
content: Experiment 3 adds Byzantine fault injection, anomaly detection, dynamic trust, and coordination/security checks to the MAPPO training setup. Agents 3 and 6 are compromised using gradual and random attacks. Over 1000 episodes, reported average reward improves from approximately -2520 in the first 50 episodes to approximately -259 in the last 50 episodes. Average trust improves from about 0.44 to about 0.58; false-positive rate is about 0.25, Byzantine detection rate is about 0.14 after the detector fix, and consensus rate is about 0.68. The run had not yet matched Experiment 2's reward within the same 1000-episode budget.

title: Experiment 3 — Why Convergence Is Slower
content: The security-enabled run slows learning because quarantined agents are prevented from receiving a normal PPO update for that step. Early in training, policies are exploratory and actions can naturally disagree with a momentary plurality. The voting-disagreement detector therefore produces many flags that are not necessarily attacks. This reduces the amount of clean policy-gradient learning signal. The finding is best described as a measurable security-versus-convergence tradeoff, not as proof that the security layer is fully optimal.

title: Experiment 3 — Detector Isolation Finding
content: A fresh rollout used to isolate detector behavior showed that voting-outlier detection produced the majority of flags: approximately 343 voting-related flags versus 54 statistical flags and 0 drift flags over one 200-step episode in the tested configuration. The interpretation was that early exploratory policies naturally disagree frequently. This should be treated as a diagnostic observation from the tested run, not a universal detector-performance claim.

title: Anomaly Detector — Three Methods
content: The anomaly detector uses multiple behavioral signals. Statistical outlier detection looks for unusual action/feature behavior; voting-disagreement tracking monitors disagreement with the relevant majority/plurality behavior; behavioral drift detection looks for changes over time. Detection results contribute to trust penalties. The implementation was revised so suspicion can decay when agreement returns, reducing the risk of permanently flagging honest agents after temporary disagreement.

title: Anomaly Detector Bug Fix — Symmetric Decay
content: An earlier implementation allowed voting-disagreement suspicion to accumulate without sufficient recovery. An honest agent that disagreed repeatedly during exploration could remain flagged even after returning to normal behavior. The fix added symmetric decay on agreement so suspicion can recover. This is important because the seven agents observe different local UE/channel states and should not be expected to take identical actions at every timestep.

title: Byzantine Fault Injection
content: The Byzantine fault module simulates compromised agents whose proposed actions can be manipulated before execution. Supported attack styles in the project include random, gradual, replay/stale-action, and opposite-action patterns, subject to what is enabled in the current experiment configuration. Experiment 3 specifically used compromised agents 3 and 6 with gradual and random attacks.

title: Trust Scoring System
content: Each MAPPO agent has a trust score bounded between 0 and 1. In the tested configuration, trust starts at 1.0, decreases when an agent is flagged or violates relevant checks, and can recover when behavior becomes consistent with trusted behavior. The configured decay rate is 0.05 and recovery rate is 0.02. When trust falls below the quarantine threshold of 0.3, the secure training logic can force that agent to defer rather than execute its learned action.

title: Consensus Engine — General Design
content: The consensus engine was designed around collecting proposed actions, weighting trusted agents more heavily, excluding agents that should not participate, and determining whether sufficient agreement exists. A 60% agreement threshold is used in the configured consensus design, with defer as the safe fallback when consensus is not reached. This is a general coordination mechanism and should not be confused with the exact execution path of Experiment 3.

title: Experiment 3 — Consensus Is Diagnostic
content: In Experiment 3, consensus is recorded primarily as a diagnostic metric because the seven agents independently control handover decisions for their respective local UE/cell contexts. There is no single global handover action that all seven agents must agree to execute. The secure execution path instead applies Byzantine corruption, trust-based quarantine, and then allows non-quarantined agents to execute their own MAPPO actions. Therefore the reported consensus_rate should not be interpreted as a percentage of all executed handovers that were globally overridden by consensus.

title: Policy Checker and Handover Policy Mismatch
content: The original handover policy checker assumed that handover should occur only when the current signal was weak. The project's reward design can legitimately favor proactive movement to a stronger neighbor even when the current signal is still acceptable. This created an architectural mismatch between the checker and the learned policy. The check was disabled in the reported Experiment 3 results after testing showed that removing it did not materially change the headline numbers.

title: RSRP Explained
content: RSRP stands for Reference Signal Received Power. It is a measure of received reference-signal power from a cell, commonly represented in dBm. Less-negative values indicate stronger received power. In this project, RSRP and relative RSRP information are used as part of the agent's local observation and for constructing the channel/handover context.

title: SINR Explained
content: SINR stands for Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio. It measures desired signal quality relative to interference and noise. Higher SINR generally indicates better radio quality. In the project, SINR is included in the agent observation and is also important to reward calculation when judging whether a handover leads to a materially better radio condition.

title: Handover Decision Logic — Conceptual Flow
content: A typical simulation step follows this conceptual flow: UE/channel state is updated; local radio observations are generated; each MAPPO actor proposes an action; secure-training logic can corrupt compromised actions and evaluate trust/anomaly conditions; quarantined agents can be forced to defer; the resulting action is applied to the local handover environment; reward and telemetry are recorded; and trust/security statistics are updated. Exact call ordering should be verified against the current code before documenting implementation details.

title: Digital Twin Dashboard
content: The dashboard provides a visual interface for the project prototype. It includes views for overall system metrics, dataset exploration, supervised-agent evaluation, train/validation/test comparisons, the seven-cell digital twin and security state, MARL training results, and a project knowledge chatbot. The dashboard backend is implemented with FastAPI and the frontend is HTML/CSS/JavaScript. Some visualizations use Plotly or project-generated image/metric files depending on the page.

title: Dashboard — Seven-Cell Digital Twin
content: The digital-twin view visualizes the seven-cell RAN scenario and security state. It can expose agent trust values and security events while the simulation runs. Byzantine fault injection and agent-state changes can be represented through dashboard controls when the corresponding backend functionality is enabled. The digital twin is a visualization and interaction layer; it should not be interpreted as a full-fidelity physical network emulator.

title: Dashboard — Training Log Endpoint
content: The FastAPI dashboard backend exposes training and project data through HTTP endpoints. The /training-log endpoint is intended to return training-log data used by the frontend. If opened directly in a browser, a large JSON response can appear as dense text; that is normal for a raw API endpoint. The frontend is expected to fetch the endpoint and turn the returned records into charts or tables.

title: Project Knowledge Chatbot
content: The knowledge assistant uses a project-specific retrieval corpus so that questions about the architecture, experiments, datasets, security mechanisms, and terminology can be answered from project material. The corpus is stored as JSON Lines, with one JSON object per chunk. Each chunk contains a stable doc_id/chunk_id, title, category, source, content, keywords, and optional metadata. Retrieval should return relevant chunks and the chatbot should distinguish documented facts from proposed or future work.

title: Knowledge Base — Status Language Rules
content: The chatbot should distinguish among implemented, tested, planned, and proposed components. Experiment 2 MAPPO training and Experiment 3 secure training are implemented experiments with reported results. PQC is a stretch goal and has not been started. Consensus exists as a module, but in Experiment 3 it is used diagnostically rather than as a universal global action override. Access control and resource allocation are broader framework goals and should not be claimed as experimentally validated MARL controllers unless new evidence is added.

title: Experiment 4 — Post-Quantum Cryptography
content: Experiment 4 is a planned stretch goal involving post-quantum cryptography for inter-agent communication. It has not been started in the reported experiments. The intended motivation is to investigate quantum-resistant protection for agent coordination messages. Any specific algorithm, library integration, latency result, or security claim should be presented as future work until implemented and evaluated.

title: Why a Lightweight Python Simulator Was Chosen
content: The team chose a lightweight Python simulator rather than making NS-3, OpenAirInterface, or srsRAN the primary simulation environment. The rationale was development time and research focus: the contribution is centered on secure multi-agent decision-making rather than building a complete network emulator. MATLAB was still used for channel-map generation where standards-oriented propagation modeling provides useful realism.

title: Technology Stack
content: The project uses Python for environment, agents, security, coordination, and dashboard backend code; PyTorch for neural-network components; a multi-agent environment interface for the RAN simulation; MATLAB/5G Toolbox for channel-map generation; pandas and matplotlib for data processing and visualization; scikit-learn for supervised baseline and selected analytics; FastAPI for the dashboard backend; and HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the dashboard frontend. Additional infrastructure such as Docker or RL orchestration libraries should only be listed as active dependencies if they are present in the current requirements/codebase.

title: Repository Structure
content: The project is organized into several technical components covering the MARL agents, coordination mechanisms, RAN environment, security layer, training and evaluation, datasets, documentation, and dashboard. A supervised ML baseline is maintained as a separate reference implementation so that conventional ML results can be compared with the sequential MARL approach. The dashboard brings these results together for visualization and comparison.

title: Ablation Study — Four Experiments
content: The ablation study is organized into four configurations. Experiment 1 is the supervised Nokia baseline. Experiment 2 is MAPPO without security. Experiment 3 is MAPPO with Byzantine/security mechanisms. Experiment 4 is the planned full system with PQC. The purpose is to isolate the incremental effect of sequential multi-agent learning and then security, while keeping the comparison honest about the different evaluation metrics.

title: Security Metrics
content: The secure experiment tracks multiple security and learning indicators: total reward, average trust score, false-positive rate, Byzantine detection rate, and consensus rate. These metrics answer different questions. Reward measures control performance; trust measures the state of the trust mechanism; false-positive rate measures incorrect suspicion; Byzantine detection rate measures attack identification in the tested setup; and consensus rate measures agreement according to the consensus diagnostic. None of these metrics alone is sufficient to establish overall security.

title: How to Interpret Experiment 3 Results
content: Experiment 3 should be reported honestly as an intermediate result: security mechanisms are active and measurable, trust improves during training, and reward improves substantially, but the run does not match the unsecured MAPPO baseline within 1000 episodes. The most defensible interpretation is that the security mechanisms introduce a learning/convergence cost in the tested setup. Possible follow-up experiments include longer training, detector warm-up/curriculum, better separation of exploration disagreement from malicious disagreement, and evaluation across multiple random seeds.

title: Recommended Next Experiments
content: Useful next experiments include extending secure training to 2000–3000 episodes, repeating both secure and unsecured runs across multiple random seeds, adding a detector warm-up period, evaluating the effect of each detector component separately, tuning the voting-disagreement threshold, and measuring performance at different Byzantine fractions. These experiments would help distinguish genuine security cost from detector sensitivity and stochastic training variation.

title: Attack Fractions and Security Evaluation
content: The security framework is intended to support evaluation under different proportions of compromised agents. Earlier project planning included 10%, 25%, and 33% Byzantine-agent fractions, while the reported Experiment 3 specifically compromises agents 3 and 6 in the seven-agent setup. Results from a particular attack fraction should not be generalized to all fractions without running those configurations.

title: References and Research Context
content: The project's literature context includes work on LLM/agentic AI for O-RAN and 6G resilience, predictive mobility, jamming-resilient handover triggering with reinforcement learning, attention-enhanced MAPPO, Byzantine-resilient distributed learning, and fault-tolerant multi-agent reinforcement learning. These references motivate the choices around RL-based mobility control, multi-agent coordination, and robustness to compromised agents. Individual paper claims should be verified against the original papers before being presented as formal literature conclusions.

title: Important Terminology — UE
content: UE means User Equipment. It refers to the end device communicating through the cellular radio network, such as a phone, modem, or other connected device. In the simulation, UEs move through the seven-cell layout and their changing radio conditions drive handover decisions.

title: Important Terminology — Ping-Pong Handover
content: Ping-pong behavior occurs when a UE switches between cells unnecessarily and then switches back soon afterward. It can waste signaling and radio resources and reduce mobility stability. The reward function penalizes unnecessary switching so that agents learn not to trigger handovers merely because a neighboring cell has a small temporary advantage.

title: Important Terminology — Radio Link Failure
content: Radio link failure (RLF) represents loss or unacceptable degradation of the radio connection. In the handover environment it is strongly penalized because a late or poor mobility decision can allow the serving link to become unusable. The reported unsecured MAPPO evaluation achieved zero RLFs in its deterministic test run.

title: Project Team Ownership
content: The project work is organized across several technical areas: RAN environment and channel simulation, MAPPO agent implementation, coordination and security mechanisms, and the monitoring/dashboard layer. These components work together as one secure multi-agent RAN control framework. Individual implementation ownership can evolve, so the project's current implementation and experiment results should be treated as the authoritative source for status.

title: Nokia Collaboration Context
content: The project is part of the Nokia Bangalore University Collaboration program. The project topic is a secure multi-agent AI framework for RAN control loops, with a working prototype and research output as goals. Nokia-provided material is used in the baseline and project validation. Intellectual-property and publication decisions should follow the governing collaboration agreement and university/Nokia guidance.

title: Chatbot Answering Policy
content: When answering questions about the project, prioritize implemented components, experiment results, configuration settings, training logs, and documented findings over assumptions. Explicitly state when a component is planned, disabled, diagnostic-only, or not yet validated. Do not invent metrics, claim convergence that was not observed, or present future PQC work as already implemented. When implementation details and high-level descriptions differ, the experimentally verified implementation behavior should take precedence.

title: Chatbot — Common Questions
content: Common questions include: What is MAPPO? Why use RL instead of an LLM? What does each agent observe? What actions can an agent take? How does Byzantine injection work? What happens when trust falls below 0.3? Why is Experiment 3 slower than Experiment 2? What do RSRP and SINR mean? What does the digital twin show? What is the difference between the Nokia supervised baseline and MARL? Is PQC implemented? The answers should be grounded in the corresponding project chunks.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is MARL?
content: MARL stands for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. It is a form of reinforcement learning where multiple agents learn to make decisions while interacting with the same environment. In our project, multiple agents independently make RAN control decisions while learning coordinated behavior.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is the main objective of this project?
content: The objective is to develop a secure multi-agent AI framework for 6G RAN control loops. The framework uses MARL to make RRC handover decisions and adds security mechanisms such as Byzantine fault injection, anomaly detection, dynamic trust, and consensus-based monitoring.

metadata.question: What is the main objective of this project?

title: Presentation Q&A — What problem are we solving in RAN?
content: We are addressing intelligent RRC handover control. As a UE moves between cells, the network must decide when it should remain connected to its current cell or hand over to a neighboring cell. Incorrect decisions can cause radio link failures, unnecessary handovers, and ping-pong effects.

metadata.question: What problem are we solving in RAN?

title: Presentation Q&A — What is RAN?
content: RAN stands for Radio Access Network. It is the part of a mobile network that connects user equipment such as phones to the cellular network through base stations or cells. Our project focuses on applying AI to control decisions within the RAN.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is RRC?
content: RRC stands for Radio Resource Control. It is responsible for controlling the connection between the UE and the radio network. In our project, the main RRC decision being studied is whether to trigger a handover and which neighboring cell to select.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is a UE?
content: UE stands for User Equipment. It refers to a device communicating with the cellular network, such as a smartphone or connected device. In our simulation, UEs move through a seven-cell RAN environment.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is a handover?
content: A handover occurs when a UE changes its serving cell while maintaining network connectivity. Our MARL agents learn when a handover should be triggered and which neighboring cell is preferable.

title: Presentation Q&A — Why is handover important?
content: Poor handover decisions can cause radio link failures, unnecessary handovers, and ping-pong effects. A good controller should hand over when another cell provides significantly better conditions while avoiding unnecessary switching.

title: Presentation Q&A — How exactly is MARL used in this project?
content: We model the RAN as a multi-agent environment with seven MAPPO agents associated with seven cells. Each agent observes local network conditions and chooses an RRC action. The agents learn through rewards based on successful handovers, healthy defer decisions, radio link failures, and ping-pong behavior.

metadata.question: How exactly is MARL used in this project?

title: Presentation Q&A — Why do we use multiple agents instead of one agent?
content: The RAN contains multiple interacting cells and UEs. A multi-agent setup allows different agents to make local decisions while learning coordinated behavior. This better represents the distributed nature of RAN control compared with one centralized decision-maker.

metadata.question: Why do we use multiple agents instead of one agent?

title: Presentation Q&A — What does each MARL agent do?
content: Each agent observes the local state of its associated cell or UE and chooses one of three actions: defer, trigger handover to the best neighbor, or trigger handover to the second-best neighbor.

metadata.question: What does each MARL agent do?

title: Presentation Q&A — What algorithm are we using?
content: We use MAPPO — Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization. MAPPO is a multi-agent extension of PPO and is well suited to cooperative multi-agent problems.

title: Presentation Q&A — Why did we choose MAPPO?
content: MAPPO provides coordinated multi-agent learning while allowing decentralized execution. It is a strong baseline for cooperative MARL and fits our scenario where multiple RAN agents need to learn compatible policies.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is CTDE?
content: CTDE stands for Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution. During training, the critic can use information from multiple agents to learn coordination. During execution, each agent uses its own local observation to make its decision.

title: Presentation Q&A — What does an agent observe?
content: Our current RAN environment uses three main observation features: SINR, delta RSRP, and NACK density. These provide information about signal quality, relative cell strength, and communication reliability.

title: Presentation Q&A — What actions can the agents take?
content: There are three actions: defer, trigger handover to the best neighboring cell, and trigger handover to the second-best neighboring cell.

metadata.question: What actions can the agents take?

title: Presentation Q&A — What is the reward function?
content: The reward encourages useful handovers and discourages harmful decisions. A successful handover to a significantly better cell gives +10, healthy defer gives +1, a radio link failure gives -10, and an unnecessary ping-pong handover gives -5.

title: Presentation Q&A — How does the agent know whether a handover was good?
content: The environment evaluates the resulting network condition, particularly the improvement in SINR. A handover to a significantly better cell receives a positive reward, while harmful or unnecessary handovers receive penalties.

metadata.question: How does the agent know whether a handover was good?

title: Presentation Q&A — Why do we need security in MARL?
content: A multi-agent system can be affected if one or more agents become compromised and start sending malicious decisions. A compromised agent could influence RAN control decisions, so our framework adds mechanisms to detect abnormal behavior and reduce the impact of compromised agents.

metadata.question: Why do we need security in MARL?

title: Presentation Q&A — What is a Byzantine attack?
content: A Byzantine attack occurs when a compromised agent behaves maliciously or inconsistently rather than following its learned policy. In our experiments, Byzantine behavior can corrupt an agent's proposed action using attack strategies such as random or gradual manipulation.

title: Presentation Q&A — Which agents are compromised in Experiment 3?
content: In the reported Experiment 3, agents 3 and 6 are compromised. They use gradual and random attack behaviors respectively.

metadata.question: Which agents are compromised in Experiment 3?

title: Presentation Q&A — What types of Byzantine attacks do we support?
content: The security framework supports random, gradual, replay, and opposite-action attack behaviors. Experiment 3 specifically uses gradual and random attacks.

metadata.question: What types of Byzantine attacks do we support?

title: Presentation Q&A — What is anomaly detection doing?
content: The anomaly detector monitors agent behavior and looks for abnormal behavior using three mechanisms: statistical outlier detection, voting disagreement tracking, and behavioral drift detection.

title: Presentation Q&A — How does trust work?
content: Each agent has a trust score between 0 and 1. Consistent behavior allows trust to recover, while anomalous or suspicious behavior causes trust to decrease. If trust falls below the quarantine threshold of 0.3, the agent is forced to defer.

title: Presentation Q&A — What happens when an agent is quarantined?
content: A quarantined agent cannot execute its own potentially unsafe action. Its action is replaced with the safe defer action. During secure training, that forced action is also excluded from the agent's PPO update so that the policy is not incorrectly credited for an action it did not choose.

metadata.question: What happens when an agent is quarantined?

title: Presentation Q&A — What is consensus?
content: Consensus is a mechanism for evaluating whether agents sufficiently agree on a proposed decision. Our general consensus design uses trust-weighted voting, excludes agents that should not participate, and requires a configured 60% agreement threshold. If consensus is not reached, defer is the safe fallback.

title: Presentation Q&A — Does consensus override every agent's action in Experiment 3?
content: No. In Experiment 3, each agent independently controls its own UE handover, so there is no single action that all seven agents need to agree on. Therefore, consensus is currently used as a diagnostic metric, while the security mechanism acts through Byzantine corruption, trust, anomaly detection, and quarantine.

metadata.question: Does consensus override every agent's action in Experiment 3?

title: Presentation Q&A — What was the anomaly detector bug we found?
content: The voting-disagreement detector originally increased suspicion when an agent disagreed with the majority but did not properly reduce suspicion when the agent returned to normal behavior. This caused honest agents to remain flagged. We fixed it by adding symmetric decay when agents agree, allowing trust and suspicion to recover.

metadata.question: What was the anomaly detector bug we found?

title: Presentation Q&A — What experiments were conducted?
content: The ablation study has four configurations: Experiment 1 is the supervised ML baseline; Experiment 2 is MAPPO without security; Experiment 3 is MAPPO with the security layer and Byzantine attacks; and Experiment 4 is the planned full system with post-quantum cryptography. Experiment 4 has not been started yet.

title: Presentation Q&A — What was Experiment 1?
content: Experiment 1 was the supervised ML baseline. Eight conventional ML agents were trained on the 70k-row RAN telemetry dataset. This provides a reference point for comparing conventional snapshot-based prediction with sequential MARL decision-making.

title: Presentation Q&A — What was Experiment 2?
content: Experiment 2 trained seven MAPPO agents without the security layer for 1000 episodes. The reward improved from approximately 867 to 1791 using 50-episode averages. Final deterministic evaluation achieved a reward of 962, 386 successful handovers, and zero radio link failures.

title: Presentation Q&A — What was Experiment 3?
content: Experiment 3 added the security stack to MAPPO, including Byzantine fault injection, anomaly detection, trust management, and consensus diagnostics. Agents 3 and 6 were compromised, and training was conducted for 1000 episodes.

title: Presentation Q&A — Why has Experiment 3 not converged yet?
content: Security mechanisms introduce a measurable training cost. During early exploration, agents naturally disagree frequently because their policies are close to random. The detector can therefore flag some legitimate exploratory behavior. Quarantined agents also skip their PPO update for that step, reducing the learning signal. As policies become more stable, disagreement should decrease and trust should recover.

metadata.question: Why has Experiment 3 not converged yet?

title: Presentation Q&A — Is Experiment 3 a failure?
content: No. Experiment 3 is trending in the correct direction but has not matched Experiment 2 within the same 1000-episode budget. The slower convergence demonstrates a measurable trade-off introduced by security mechanisms, which is itself an important ablation finding.

title: Presentation Q&A — What were the Experiment 3 results?
content: Across 1000 episodes, average total reward improved from approximately -2520 in the first 50 episodes to -259 in the last 50 episodes. Average trust increased from about 0.44 to 0.58, while Byzantine detection rate was approximately 0.14 and consensus rate approximately 0.68.

title: Presentation Q&A — What is Experiment 4?
content: Experiment 4 is a planned full-system experiment with Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The goal is to investigate quantum-resistant protection for inter-agent communication. It has not been started yet and is currently a stretch goal.

title: Presentation Q&A — What datasets are we using?
content: We use two main sources. First, a 70k-row RAN telemetry dataset for supervised baseline and security-related analysis. Second, synthetic channel data generated using a 3GPP TR 38.901 Urban Macro model, including RSRP and SINR maps for the seven-cell scenario.

title: Presentation Q&A — What are RSRP and SINR?
content: RSRP measures the received reference signal strength from a cell, while SINR measures signal quality relative to interference and noise. In our environment, RSRP-related information contributes to the agent's observations, while SINR is important for evaluating whether a handover improves the connection.

title: Presentation Q&A — Why did we build a lightweight RAN simulator?
content: Our primary research contribution is the secure multi-agent AI framework, rather than developing a complete network simulator. A lightweight Python environment allows us to model the required RAN behavior and train the agents without spending most of the project timeline integrating a much heavier network simulator.

metadata.question: Why did we build a lightweight RAN simulator?

title: Presentation Q&A — What is the digital twin/dashboard used for?
content: The dashboard provides a visual interface for monitoring the system. It shows network and agent metrics, training behavior, security information, and the seven-cell digital twin. It also helps demonstrate how trust, Byzantine behavior, RAN conditions, and MARL performance change during experiments.
